title: Most Roman doctors hold some sins venial by nature—yet not as a defined article of faith
source_text: LVII. Porro ex iis quae Thesibus hisce & superioribus exposita fuerunt, patet longe maximam partem Doctorum Scholae Romanae statuere communi consensu, quod sint quaedam peccata quae per se & sua natura non sunt mortalia, sed venialia: quo-niam per se reatum mortis aeternae non inducunt; nec animae vitam spiritualem, quae in Dei amore & gratia consistit, extinguunt: Veruntamen istud apud eos nondum haberi pro fidei articulo, & re plane certa atque definita: quia in Schola Romana Theologi nonnulli sunt, & quidem ex celeberrimis, qui contrarium tenent, & qui peccata omnia per se & sua natura mortalia esse existimant, nec ulla esse venialia cen-sent, nisi per Dei clementiam & misericordiam.
pass_a_gloss: Further from those things which have been set forth in these and the preceding Theses it is plain that by far the greatest part of the Doctors of the Roman School establish by common consent that there are certain sins which of themselves and by their own nature are not mortal but venial: since of themselves they do not induce the guilt of eternal death; nor extinguish the soul’s spiritual life which consists in the love and grace of God. Nevertheless that is not yet held among them for an article of faith and a matter plainly certain and defined: because in the Roman School there are some theologians, and those among the most celebrated, who hold the contrary, and who judge all sins to be of themselves and by their nature mortal, and think none venial except through God’s clemency and mercy.
pass_b_english: Dominant Roman school: some sins venial by nature—no eternal-death guilt, no extinguished spiritual life.
Not yet a defined article: celebrated Roman voices still hold every sin mortal of itself, venial only by mercy.

lemmas.gloss: of themselves and by their nature
